stat.text: 51% of US public company directors say keeping pace with AI is their board's top challenge for the next 12 months (BDO 2026 Board Survey).

podcast_brief:
## The day in one line

It is a short news day, and artificial intelligence runs through most of it. A large survey of American directors finds AI at the top of the boardroom worry list, even as a meaningful share of boards admit they lack a framework to oversee it. Around that, Canada adds more Russia sanctions and France's privacy regulator keeps up a steady stream of small penalties for weak cybersecurity.

## Story 1 — Boards rank AI as their top challenge, but one in five lack a framework to oversee it

**The facts.**
- BDO USA published its 2026 Board Survey on October 19. It is based on responses from more than 200 directors of US public companies across many industries, gathered in June 2026. The trade press picked it up again this past week.
- The headline number: 51% of directors say keeping pace with AI and emerging technologies is their board's top challenge for the next 12 months. That is well ahead of the next items, balancing competing agenda priorities (36%) and deciding where to put limited capital (35%).
- Looking at the external environment over the next six to 12 months, 57% name the speed of change in AI and cyber capabilities as a significant concern. That ranks above changes to tariffs, sanctions and trade policy (46%), regulatory uncertainty tied to the US midterm elections (41%) and geopolitical conflict (38%). Concern about geopolitics varies a lot by company size: 65% of large-cap directors cite it, against 27% at mid-cap companies.
- On readiness, 20% say their board has no clear governance framework for overseeing AI adoption and cybersecurity risk. Only 36% are very confident their board has the right skills to oversee AI, cybersecurity and data governance, 49% are somewhat confident and 15% are not confident. Reporting on the survey, CIO Dive noted that 88% are confident their executives can identify and manage emerging technology and cyber risk, which suggests boards are leaning heavily on management.
- Demand for expertise is moving quickly. 49% rank technology and innovation as the most sought-after skill for new board members, up from 42% in 2025. 45% prioritise cybersecurity and data protection expertise, up from 35%.
- The survey also shows boards rating their own governance less highly. 42% say board effectiveness work, meaning evaluations, refreshment, structure and director education, is the area most likely to be deprioritised. 22% now call their board ineffective at crisis response, up from 13% a year ago. 20% say it is ineffective at evaluations and refreshment, up from 9%. The share calling their collaboration with the CEO and management highly effective fell from 69% to 58%.
- CIO Dive also reported that about a quarter of directors said growing agenda complexity had led them to give AI and cybersecurity oversight lower priority.
- Amy Rojik, who leads BDO USA's corporate governance practice, framed the results around focus, saying directors need to be "deliberate about where they focus their attention."
- Some limits are worth stating plainly. The published materials give no margin of error or detailed methodology, and the sample is a little over 200 people. The numbers show direction and how directors see themselves. They are not a precise measurement of every board in the US.

**Background.**
- BDO runs this survey every year. Its 2025 edition found boards struggling to move from adopting AI to integrating it into the business, so the AI theme is not new. What changed this year is how far AI has pulled ahead of other challenges, and the drop in how directors rate their own processes.
- In US corporate law, directors have a recognised duty to oversee risks that are central to the business. Delaware case law has made clear in recent years that a board with no reporting system for a mission-critical risk can face personal claims. As AI moves into products, hiring, customer service and financial reporting, more companies treat it as that kind of risk.
- Regulators in several jurisdictions, including the EU through its AI Act, have created obligations that reach the board through accountability and documentation requirements.

**Who's affected.**
- Directors of public companies in every industry, and especially their audit, risk and technology committees.
- General counsel and corporate secretaries, who design board agendas, reporting lines and committee charters.
- Chief compliance officers and risk leaders, who supply much of the information boards use to oversee AI and cyber risk.
- Nominating and governance committees, which are under pressure to add technology and cyber expertise.

**What it does not change.**
- The survey is a measure of opinion. It creates no new legal duty and is not regulatory guidance.

**Why it matters.** The survey captures a gap between how much directors worry about AI and how ready they say they are to oversee it. If a fifth of boards lack a framework and many lack confidence in their own skills, the quality of what management brings to the board matters more. The weaker scores for crisis response and board evaluations are notable too, because those are the processes plaintiffs and regulators look at first after something goes wrong.

**How this comes up with a GC or CLO.** General counsel are likely to mention this survey when discussing what their board is asking for, often more regular, structured reporting on where AI is used and what could go wrong. Chief compliance officers may raise it in the context of who owns AI risk between legal, compliance, technology and the business, and how that ownership is shown to directors.

**Questions a buyer might ask.**
- How many boards say they have no clear framework for overseeing AI and cyber risk, and is that number moving?
- Are directors relying more on management's assurances than on their own expertise?
- What does the drop in crisis-response ratings say about how ready boards are for an AI-related incident?

## Story 2 — Canada imposes additional sanctions on Russia to reduce its missile capabilities

**The facts.**
- Canada's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Anita Anand, announced a new round of sanctions on Russia under the Special Economic Measures (Russia) Regulations.
- The announcement was made on the margins of the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris.
- The government says the measures aim to reduce Russia's missile capabilities and raise the economic costs of its war against Ukraine. The candidate material available to us does not list the individual names, entities or goods added, so the exact scope is not covered here.

**Background.**
- Canada has used its Special Economic Measures Act against Russia since 2014, after the annexation of Crimea, and has added names in many rounds since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Canadian rounds often target defence suppliers, the energy sector, the so-called shadow fleet of tankers and the networks that help Russia obtain components.
- G7 meetings are a common moment for allies to announce coordinated sanctions, so similar steps from other G7 members around the same time would not be unusual.

**Who's affected.**
- Canadian banks, insurers, shippers, manufacturers and exporters, and any person in Canada or Canadian abroad dealing with listed parties.
- Compliance teams that screen customers, suppliers and payments against the consolidated Canadian list.
- Companies whose supply chains include dual-use goods or components that could reach Russian weapons production.

**Why it matters.** Each new listing changes the list of parties that sanctions screening has to catch, sometimes overnight. Measures aimed at missile capability usually reach beyond well-known state firms to intermediaries, traders and component suppliers in third countries. Those are hard to spot without good information on who owns and controls a counterparty. Canadian sanctions also carry criminal penalties, and enforcement has been growing.

**How this comes up with a GC or CLO.** Compliance leaders at Canadian companies with international supply chains tend to raise new rounds like this when discussing how fast their screening picks up list changes and how far down the supply chain their due diligence goes. Legal teams may also ask about how Canadian measures line up with US, UK and EU sanctions.

**Questions a buyer might ask.**
- How quickly do new Canadian listings appear in the lists companies screen against?
- How does a company show it checked indirect links, such as distributors or freight agents, to sanctioned parties?

## Story 3 — AI is prompting new legal risks in the workplace

**The facts.**
- Corporate Compliance Insights published an analysis on new legal risks arising from the use of AI in the workplace.
- Its central point is that the use of AI, particularly by company leaders, can increase legal exposure for employers.
- The piece is commentary, not a report of a specific case or new rule. The details of the article's examples are not in the material we have, so this summary stays at the level of its main argument.

**Background.**
- Employers have used automated tools in hiring and performance management for years, and regulators have repeatedly said existing anti-discrimination laws apply to decisions made with them. Several US states and cities have passed their own rules on automated employment decisions, and the EU AI Act classes many employment uses of AI as high risk.
- The newer angle is leadership behaviour: managers and executives using generative AI to draft performance reviews, summarise investigations, assess staff or make decisions about people. Those uses can create records, bias questions and confidentiality issues that land on the employer.

**Who's affected.**
- Employment lawyers and HR leaders in companies of every size.
- Compliance teams that run investigations or handle speak-up reports, where AI-generated summaries or decisions could later be challenged.
- Senior managers whose own use of AI tools may not be covered by existing policies.

**Why it matters.** The argument moves AI risk from technology projects to everyday management behaviour. When a leader relies on an AI tool in a decision about a person, the employer may have to explain that decision in a discrimination claim, a retaliation case or a regulator's inquiry. That raises questions of policy coverage, training and documentation that many companies have not settled.

**How this comes up with a GC or CLO.** Employment counsel may bring this up when discussing whether the company's AI use policy covers executives as well as frontline staff. Compliance leaders may connect it to investigations, asking whether AI tools used to summarise or assess complaints could weaken the fairness of a process.

**Questions a buyer might ask.**
- Does the company know which managers use AI in decisions about employees?
- Could an AI-drafted performance review or investigation summary become evidence in a retaliation claim?

## Story 4 — CNIL issues ten sanctions against French local authorities over cybersecurity failings

**The facts.** France's data protection authority, the CNIL, said it imposed ten sanctions in November 2026 under its simplified procedure on local authorities and one public body, all for cybersecurity failings.

**Background.** The simplified procedure, available since 2022, lets the CNIL handle less complex cases quickly with capped fines. Earlier this year it said it had issued 23 simplified sanctions since January.

**Who's affected.** French municipalities and public bodies, and by example any organisation holding personal data with weak basic security.

**Why it matters.** The CNIL is treating basic security failures as routine enforcement matters rather than rare, large cases.

**How it comes up.** Privacy and compliance leaders may cite it as evidence that European regulators are penalising security basics, not only major breaches.

**One question.** Does the fast-track route mean more frequent, smaller penalties for basic security gaps?

## Story 5 — EU leaders to discuss AI challenges

**The facts.** Euractiv's technology newsletter reports that EU leaders are set to discuss the challenges posed by AI. The same edition covers CAIDA, TikTok's recommendation algorithm and Poland's Kids Act. Further detail is not in the material available.

**Background.** The EU AI Act is being phased in, and the Commission has been under pressure to simplify parts of its digital rulebook. Heads of government taking up AI signals that the debate has reached the highest political level.

**Who's affected.** Companies that build or deploy AI in the EU, and their legal teams.

**Why it matters.** Political decisions at leader level can change the timing or shape of obligations companies are preparing for.

**How it comes up.** General counsel with EU operations may mention it when discussing how settled AI Act timelines really are.

**One question.** Could leader-level talks shift the timing of AI Act obligations?

bdo-board-survey-0911.headline: Boards rank AI as their top challenge, but one in five lack a framework to oversee it
bdo-board-survey-0911.dek: BDO's 2026 survey of more than 200 US public company directors finds rising AI anxiety alongside weaker ratings for board self-governance.
bdo-board-survey-0911.body_md:
Keeping up with artificial intelligence has become the leading worry in American boardrooms. BDO USA's 2026 Board Survey found that 51% of public company directors name keeping pace with AI and emerging technologies as their top challenge for the next 12 months. The survey also points to signs of strain in how boards govern themselves.

The professional services firm released the annual survey on October 19. It drew on responses from more than 200 public company directors across a range of industries, collected in June 2026, according to BDO and to coverage in CIO Dive.

### Key findings

- **AI tops the agenda.** 51% call keeping pace with AI their main challenge, ahead of balancing competing agenda priorities (36%) and capital allocation under resource limits (35%). 57% list the speed of change in AI and cyber capabilities among their biggest external concerns, ahead of trade, tariff and sanctions policy (46%), regulatory uncertainty linked to the US midterm elections (41%) and geopolitical conflict (38%).
- **Oversight gaps.** One in five directors (20%) say their board lacks a clear governance framework for overseeing AI adoption and cybersecurity risk. Only 36% are very confident their board has the skills to oversee AI, cybersecurity and data governance, and 15% are not confident.
- **Skills in demand.** 49% rank technology and innovation as the expertise boards most need, up from 42% in 2025. 45% prioritise cybersecurity and data protection, up from 35%.
- **Self-governance slipping.** 42% say board effectiveness work, such as evaluations, refreshment and education, may be deprioritised. 22% rate their board ineffective at crisis response, up from 13% a year earlier. 20% say the same about evaluations and refreshment, up from 9%. The share rating collaboration with management as highly effective fell to 58% from 69%.

CIO Dive also reported that roughly a quarter of directors said growing agenda complexity had pushed AI and cybersecurity oversight down their list. BDO's leader for corporate governance, Amy Rojik, said effective governance increasingly requires directors to be "deliberate about where they focus their attention."

### Background

Courts and regulators have long held directors responsible for overseeing mission-critical risks, and AI is now treated as one of them. BDO's 2025 survey had already found boards struggling to move from AI adoption to integration. This year's results suggest that concern about AI is growing faster than the governance structures meant to handle it.

### What this means for legal and compliance leaders

The survey shows a gap between how much directors worry about AI and how ready their boards say they are to oversee it. A board that lacks a framework, or is unsure of its own skills, relies more heavily on management reporting. That makes general counsel and compliance leaders a primary channel for AI risk information. The fall in ratings for crisis readiness and board evaluations also matters, because both tend to be examined closely after a failure.

### Questions you may hear

- How many boards say they have no clear framework for overseeing AI and cyber risk?
- Is AI oversight being pushed down the board agenda as other pressures build?
- Which skills are boards trying to add, and how fast is that demand growing?
